coreConcept: Describe the basic principles and role of surgery in cancer management, including its use for curative and palliative purposes

coreConcept: Describe the basic principles and role of surgery in cancer management, including its use for curative and palliative purposes
statement: What is the clinical significance of the 'no-touch' technique during tumor excision?
options: It minimizes the amount of blood loss during the dissection of major vessels.
It reduces the risk of accidental surgical instrument contamination with bacteria.
It shortens the recovery time by reducing the overall inflammatory response.
It prevents the intraoperative dissemination of tumor cells into the circulation.
It avoids damaging the surrounding nerves and preserving the patient's function.
correctOption: It prevents the intraoperative dissemination of tumor cells into the circulation.
optionExplanations: Blood loss is controlled by hemostasis, not the 'no-touch' oncologic principle.
This refers to sepsis prevention, not the oncologic 'no-touch' principle.
While it might reduce inflammation, the primary goal is preventing recurrence/spread.
The no-touch technique aims to prevent handling from squeezing cancer cells into vessels.
Nerve preservation is a different principle (functional preservation).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 155 (Book Page): Ref Text Excerpt: taking care not to disrupt the primary tumour at the time of excision is of the utmost importance in obtaining a cure in localised disease and in preventing local recurrence.

coreConcept: Describe the basic principles and role of surgery in cancer management, including its use for curative and palliative purposes
statement: Which statement best describes the removal of primary disease in localized cancer?
options: It is only indicated if the patient has no symptoms related to the primary mass.
It requires meticulous surgery to avoid disrupting the tumor during excision.
It involves only the removal of the macroscopic tumor without any margins.
It is always performed after a course of systemic therapy regardless of stage.
It is considered a palliative measure in the majority of early-stage solid tumors.
correctOption: It requires meticulous surgery to avoid disrupting the tumor during excision.
optionExplanations: Symptoms often provide the indication for surgery, though asymptomatic masses are removed too.
Avoiding tumor disruption (spillage) is essential for a curative outcome.
Macroscopic removal only (R2 resection) is usually inadequate for cure.
Surgery is often the first-line treatment for localized solid tumors.
Surgery for early-stage solid tumors is primarily curative, not palliative.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 165 (Book Page): Ref Text Excerpt: meticulous surgery taking care not to disrupt the primary tumour at the time of excision is of the utmost importance in obtaining a cure in localised disease.

coreConcept: Describe the basic principles and role of surgery in cancer management, including its use for curative and palliative purposes
statement: What role does surgery play in the prevention of cancer for specific patients?
options: Systematic removal of the appendix in all children to prevent appendiceal cancer.
Mass screening of the population using diagnostic laparoscopy once a decade.
Periodic biopsy of healthy tissues to detect microscopic changes before a mass.
Removal of healthy organs in patients with a high genetic risk of malignancy.
Routine excision of all benign skin moles to prevent melanoma transformation.
correctOption: Removal of healthy organs in patients with a high genetic risk of malignancy.
optionExplanations: Appendiceal cancer is too rare to justify systematic prophylactic appendectomy.
Laparoscopy is too invasive for screening; non-invasive tests are preferred.
Biopsy is diagnostic for existing disease, not a preventative measure for healthy tissue.
Prophylactic surgery (e.g., mastectomy or colectomy) is a preventative role for surgery.
Only atypical or changing moles are removed; routine excision of all moles is not standard.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 158 (Book Page): Ref Text Excerpt: However, surgery has several roles in cancer treatment including diagnosis, removal of primary disease... prevention and reconstruction.

coreConcept: Describe the basic principles and role of surgery in cancer management, including its use for curative and palliative purposes
statement: In which condition might surgery for metastatic disease be considered appropriate?
options: Isolated liver metastases from a primary colorectal carcinoma that is controlled.
Multi-focal brain metastases from a primary small cell carcinoma of the lung.
Bilateral adrenal metastases from a widely disseminated malignant melanoma.
Diffuse pleural thickening and effusion from a primary mesothelioma of lung.
Extensive bone marrow involvement in a patient with acute myeloid leukemia.
correctOption: Isolated liver metastases from a primary colorectal carcinoma that is controlled.
optionExplanations: Resection of isolated liver/lung metastases can be curative or prolong survival in CRC.
SCLC is systemic; surgery is rarely indicated for brain metastases in this context.
Bilateral/widespread metastases in melanoma are treated systemically.
Mesothelioma is generally treated with multimodality therapy; surgery is rarely for 'metastasis'.
Leukemia is a non-solid, systemic malignancy; surgery has no role in bone marrow.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 155 (Book Page): Ref Text Excerpt: Under certain circumstances surgery for metastatic disease may be appropriate... particularly from renal cell carcinoma [and others].

coreConcept: Describe the basic principles and role of surgery in cancer management, including its use for curative and palliative purposes
statement: Radical surgery involves removal of the primary tumor and which other components?
options: The skin overlying the tumor and the underlying bone in all clinical cases.
Surrounding tissue and the regional lymph node drainage of the primary site.
Only the palpable lymph nodes that are enlarged on clinical physical exam.
Distant organs that are commonly known to be sites of metastatic spread.
The entire organ of origin regardless of the size or location of the tumor.
correctOption: Surrounding tissue and the regional lymph node drainage of the primary site.
optionExplanations: Bone and skin are only removed if directly involved by the tumor.
This definition of radical surgery ensures both local and regional control.
Regional drainage is removed regardless of palpability to clear microscopic nodes.
This describes metastasectomy or exenteration, not the standard 'radical surgery'.
Organ removal (total vs partial) depends on margins and site, not just 'radicality'.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 165 (Book Page): Ref Text Excerpt: Radical surgery for cancer involves removal of the primary tumour and as much of the surrounding tissue and lymph node drainage as possible

coreConcept: Describe the basic principles and role of surgery in cancer management, including its use for curative and palliative purposes
statement: A patient presents with a suspicious lump; when is a surgical biopsy indicated?
options: Only after the patient has failed a trial of broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy.
When the diagnosis cannot be definitively established by non-invasive means.
As a routine procedure for every patient who presents with any physical lump.
When the patient requests surgery for cosmetic reasons despite a benign biopsy.
When the tumor is clearly metastatic and the primary site is already known.
correctOption: When the diagnosis cannot be definitively established by non-invasive means.
optionExplanations: Antibiotics are used for infection, but surgery shouldn't be delayed if cancer is suspected.
Surgery is a key tool in the diagnostic pathway when other tests are inconclusive.
Not all lumps require surgical biopsy; some are diagnosed by FNA or imaging.
Cosmetic requests are not the primary 'oncologic' principle of surgical biopsy.
If the primary is known and the patient has metastases, biopsy of every lump is unnecessary.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 154 (Book Page): Ref Text Excerpt: In most cases the diagnosis of cancer has been made before definitive surgery is carried out but occasionally a surgical [procedure is needed for diagnosis].
